llm_response.content:
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Cross-sectional instrumental-variables (2SLS) design.

Why IV?  
•  The treatment, “slave‐export intensity”, is plausibly endogenous: areas that were already richer, more politically centralised, or better located may both have shipped more slaves and have higher (or lower) income today.  
•  The question is long-run and country-level; there is no obvious discontinuity, policy shock, or panel structure for DID/event-study work.  
•  A valid instrument can exploit the fact that demand for African slaves was determined offshore by plantation booms and sailing technology, while the supply side (which African coast or interior could be raided) was largely a function of exogenous geography.  

Core idea of the instrument (“predicted slave exports”):  
  PredictedExports_c = Σ_t (GlobalDemand_t × VoyageFeasibility_c × RouteProximity_c)  
where  
  GlobalDemand_t = total slaves embarked worldwide in decade t (from shipping records),  
  VoyageFeasibility_c = 1/Great-circle distance from country c’s coast to the nearest major importing region in decade t (Americas, North Africa, Gulf, Indian Ocean plantation islands),  
  RouteProximity_c = prevailing wind/current favourability dummy for c’s coastline.  

This is a Bartik/shift-share style instrument: (i) the “shift” is decade-specific global demand, completely external to any individual African country, and (ii) the “share” is time-invariant geographic sailing feasibility. Because only geography enters the share, the exclusion restriction is more credible than if we used pre-slave-trade economic variables for shares.  

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_c = ln(1 + slaves exported from country c 1400–1900) / land area.  
(A continuous dose; adding 1 avoids log(0).)

Control group / counterfactual  
Countries with very low or zero predicted exports provide implicit controls. In estimation, identification comes from the continuous cross-country variation in T_c induced by the instrument.

Timing  
Exposure: cumulative 1400–1900.  
Outcome: log real GDP per capita in 2000.

No RDD running variable or cutoff is involved.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance – PredictedExports_c is strongly correlated with actual exports.  
  Plausibility: Slave-ship captains optimised sailing costs; distance, winds, and currents are first-order determinants of where slaves could be procured cheaply. Pilot checks (first-stage F ≫ 10) can verify strength.

A2. Instrument exogeneity – Conditional on controls, distance/wind-based voyage feasibility affects 2000 GDP only through the volume of slaves extracted.  
  Plausibility concerns: (i) Coastal geography might influence modern trade openness; (ii) Distance to the Americas could matter for colonial penetration. We will include an extensive geography and colonisation control set and run over-identification tests with alternative instruments (e.g., distance to Barbados for Atlantic trade only) to bolster this assumption.

A3. Monotonicity – Countries with better sailing feasibility never exported fewer slaves in response to higher global demand than countries with worse feasibility. Historically, all coasts faced rising capture pressure when demand expanded, making this assumption believable.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers) – One country’s slave extraction does not directly alter another’s modern GDP after conditioning on its own extraction. This is imperfect (regional spillovers possible) but the continent-wide scale and robustness checks with spatial lags help.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Omitted geographic or colonial factors correlated with both the instrument and modern GDP.  
  Fix: Control set (latitude, ruggedness, soil quality, malaria ecology, distance to coast, coloniser dummies, legal origin, resource wealth). Test sensitivity using Oster (2019) δ.

Threat 2: Measurement error in slave export totals (attenuation bias in OLS, bias in IV if error correlated with instrument).  
  Fix: Use multiple data sources; conduct SIMEX-style correction; replicate with alternative treatment variable (exports/1400 pop, or ethnic-level export intensity aggregated to country).

Threat 3: Small sample (N ≈ 52) → weak instruments, over-fitting of controls.  
  Fix: Report weak-IV-robust Anderson–Rubin p-values and F-stats; use limited control sets in main table, add controls progressively; use jackknife IV (JIVE) as robustness.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
############################################################
# 0. Packages
############################################################
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)       # fast OLS / IV with HC/se clustering
library(ivpack)       # weak-IV diagnostics
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

############################################################
# 1. Data Loading
############################################################
d <- read_csv("africa_slaveGDP_data.csv")   # one row per country

############################################################
# 2. Variable Construction
############################################################
d <- d %>% 
  mutate(
    ln_slaves_area   = log(1 + slaves_total) / land_area,          # treatment
    ln_pred_slaves   = log(1 + pred_slaves_total) / land_area,     # instrument
    ln_gdppc2000     = log(gdppc2000),
    controls_basic   = 1)                                          # placeholder

############################################################
# 3. Main Specification  (2SLS)
############################################################
# First-stage
fs <- feols(ln_slaves_area ~ ln_pred_slaves + latitude + rugged + 
              malaria_ecology + colonizer + legal_origin + 
              ln_population1400, data = d, se = "HC1")
summary(fs)

# Second-stage
iv_main <- feols(ln_gdppc2000 ~ 1 | ln_slaves_area ~ ln_pred_slaves |
                   latitude + rugged + malaria_ecology + colonizer + 
                   legal_origin + ln_population1400, data = d, se = "HC1")
etable(fs, iv_main, dict = c(ln_slaves_area = "Ln slave exports / area",
                             ln_pred_slaves = "Predicted ln exports",
                             ln_gdppc2000  = "Ln GDP pc 2000"))

############################################################
# 4. Robustness: Alternative Instrument (distance to Barbados)
############################################################
iv_alt <- feols(ln_gdppc2000 ~ 1 | ln_slaves_area ~ ln_pred_slaves_barbados |
                  latitude + rugged + malaria_ecology + colonizer + 
                  legal_origin + ln_population1400, data = d, se = "HC1")
etable(iv_main, iv_alt)

############################################################
# 5. Weak-IV test
############################################################
ivpack::weakivtest(iv_main)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------
Sign: Negative. Higher slave extraction intensity should depress modern GDP.  

Magnitude (back-of-envelope): A one-standard-deviation increase in log-slave exports (~1.5 s.d.) could lower 2000 GDP per capita by roughly 25–35 percent (≈ 0.3 log points). This aligns with the intuition that countries in the top quartile of historical extraction—e.g., Benin, Angola—have contemporary incomes roughly one-third those of otherwise similar low-extraction countries (e.g., Botswana).

Channels: We anticipate that ≥50 % of the total effect operates through greater ethnic fractionalisation and weaker 19th-century state centralisation, measurable via mediation analysis.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Relevance (first-stage F > 10) ...................... 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable after controls ..... 0.5  
C3: Monotonicity (no defiers) ........................... 1  
C4: SUTVA / no cross-country spillovers ................. 0.5  
C5: Correct functional form / linear first stage ........ 1  

Total = 4 out of 5 (good, but we remain cautious about exclusion and spillovers).

------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
